name: SQL & Relational Databases
description: Joins, indexes, normalisation, transactions and the query patterns that separate fast schemas from slow ones.

modules.name: Querying
modules.description: Joins, grouping, NULL semantics and the order the engine actually evaluates your query in.

cards.prompt: In what logical order are the clauses of a SELECT evaluated?
cards.answer: FROM and JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT (including window functions) → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT.
cards.explanation: This explains two everyday puzzles: you cannot use a SELECT alias in WHERE (it does not exist yet) but you can in ORDER BY; and HAVING filters groups while WHERE filters rows — so row-level conditions belong in WHERE, where they cut work earlier.

cards.prompt: INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN
cards.answer: INNER keeps only rows with a match on both sides; LEFT keeps every left row, filling the right side with NULLs when there is no match.

left.title: INNER JOIN
points: The default when both sides are required

right.title: LEFT JOIN
points: A WHERE on the right table silently turns it into an inner join
Use IS NULL on the right key to find non-matches

cards.explanation: The classic bug: `LEFT JOIN orders o ... WHERE o.status = 'paid'` discards the very rows the LEFT JOIN was preserving, because NULL fails the predicate. Put that condition in the ON clause instead.

cards.prompt: The table `t` has 3 rows and `col` is NULL in one of them. What does this return?
cards.code:
SELECT
  COUNT(*)                                          AS a,
  COUNT(col)                                        AS b,
  SUM(CASE WHEN col = NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)       AS c
FROM t;
cards.answer: 3, 2, 0 — COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(col) skips NULLs, and `col = NULL` is never true (it is UNKNOWN), so the CASE never fires.
cards.explanation: NULL is 'unknown', not a value, and comparisons with it yield UNKNOWN rather than TRUE or FALSE. Test with `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`. It also means `NOT IN (subquery)` returns nothing at all if the subquery contains a single NULL.

cards.prompt: You need each employee's salary alongside their department average, without collapsing the rows. How?
cards.answer: A window function: `AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department)`. It computes per partition but keeps every row, unlike GROUP BY.
cards.explanation: Windows also give ranking (`ROW_NUMBER`, `RANK`, `DENSE_RANK`), offsets (`LAG`, `LEAD`) and running totals with frame clauses. `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY x ORDER BY y)` filtered to 1 is the standard 'latest row per group' idiom.

cards.prompt: What performance anti-pattern is this, and what fixes it?
cards.answer: The N+1 query problem — 1 query plus 100 more. Fix with a JOIN, an eager-load/`IN (...)` batch, or a dataloader that batches per request.
cards.explanation: Each round trip costs network latency, so 101 queries at 1 ms is 100 ms of pure waiting. ORMs cause this silently through lazy relations; log query counts per request and alert when they scale with result size.

resources.title: Use The Index, Luke — N+1 selects

cards.prompt: CTE (`WITH`) vs subquery
cards.answer: They are usually equivalent to the planner; CTEs win on readability and enable recursion.

left.title: CTE
points: Named steps read top to bottom
Historically an optimisation fence in Postgres < 12

right.title: Subquery
points: Correlated subqueries can be per-row expensive
Fine for one-off filters and EXISTS

cards.explanation: Modern Postgres inlines non-recursive CTEs unless you write `MATERIALIZED`, so prefer whichever reads better. `EXISTS` usually beats `IN` for correlated existence checks, and avoids the NULL trap of `NOT IN`.

modules.name: Schema, Indexes & Transactions
modules.description: Normalisation, index design, ACID and isolation levels.

cards.prompt: What do 1NF, 2NF and 3NF require?
cards.answer: 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups. 2NF: 1NF plus no partial dependency on part of a composite key. 3NF: 2NF plus no transitive dependency — non-key columns depend on the key, the whole key and nothing but the key.
cards.explanation: Normalisation removes update anomalies by storing each fact once. Denormalise deliberately and later, for measured read performance, accepting that you now own the consistency problem — usually with triggers, materialised views or an async pipeline.

cards.prompt: You have an index on `(a, b, c)`. Which of these can use it: `WHERE a = 1`, `WHERE b = 2`, `WHERE a = 1 AND b = 2`, `WHERE a = 1 AND c = 3`?
cards.answer: The first, third and fourth can use it (the fourth only for the `a` prefix, then filters on c). `WHERE b = 2` alone cannot — a composite index is only usable from its leftmost column.
cards.explanation: The index is sorted by a, then b within a, then c. Without a, the b values are scattered. This 'leftmost prefix' rule decides how many indexes you actually need — one on (a,b,c) also serves queries on (a) and (a,b).

resources.title: Use The Index, Luke — Concatenated indexes

cards.prompt: What does an index cost you?
cards.answer: Storage, and write amplification — every INSERT, UPDATE of an indexed column and DELETE must maintain every index. It can also be ignored by the planner if it is not selective enough.
cards.explanation: A table with ten indexes writes eleven structures per insert. Drop unused indexes (`pg_stat_user_indexes` shows scans), and remember that a low-selectivity index — a boolean on a huge table — is often slower than a sequential scan.

cards.prompt: A query is slow in production. What is your first move?
cards.answer: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` it. Look for sequential scans on large tables, row-estimate errors, nested loops over big inputs, and sorts or hashes spilling to disk.
cards.explanation: EXPLAIN shows the plan; ANALYZE runs it and shows actual rows and timing. A large gap between estimated and actual rows means stale statistics — run ANALYZE or raise the statistics target before blaming the query.

cards.prompt: What does ACID stand for?
cards.answer: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (constraints hold before and after), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not see each other's intermediate state), Durability (committed data survives a crash).
cards.explanation: Atomicity comes from write-ahead logging and undo, durability from fsync-ed WAL, isolation from locking or MVCC. Consistency is the one the database only partly owns — your constraints and application invariants define it.

cards.prompt: Name the four isolation levels and the anomaly each prevents.
cards.answer: Read uncommitted (allows dirty reads), read committed (prevents dirty reads), repeatable read (also prevents non-repeatable reads), serializable (also prevents phantoms — equivalent to some serial order).
cards.explanation: Defaults differ: Postgres and Oracle use read committed, MySQL InnoDB uses repeatable read. Postgres's repeatable read is snapshot isolation, which still permits write skew — the reason `SERIALIZABLE` or explicit `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` exists.

cards.prompt: What is wrong here, and what is the only correct fix?
cards.code:
query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '{email}'"
db.execute(query)
cards.answer: SQL injection. The only reliable fix is a parameterised query — `db.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ?", (email,))` — so the value can never be parsed as SQL.
cards.explanation: Escaping by hand fails against encoding tricks and multi-byte charsets. Parameterisation separates code from data at the protocol level. Where identifiers must be dynamic (table or column names), validate against a strict allowlist — those cannot be parameterised.

resources.title: OWASP — SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet

cards.prompt: The second debit violates the CHECK constraint. What does this print?
cards.code:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(':memory:', isolation_level=None)   # autocommit; we control transactions
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE accounts (name TEXT PRIMARY KEY, balance INT CHECK (balance >= 0));
INSERT INTO accounts VALUES ('ada', 100), ('bob', 50);
""")
try:
    db.execute('BEGIN')
    db.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 80 WHERE name = 'bob'")
    db.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 80 WHERE name = 'ada'")
    db.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 80 WHERE name = 'ada'")  # violates CHECK
    db.execute('COMMIT')
except sqlite3.IntegrityError:
    db.execute('ROLLBACK')
print(db.execute('SELECT name, balance FROM accounts ORDER BY name').fetchall())
cards.explanation: Statements between `BEGIN` and `COMMIT` succeed or fail as a unit: on any error, `ROLLBACK` undoes every change in the transaction, including the credit to bob that had already run. Without an explicit transaction, most drivers autocommit each statement, so a failure half-way leaves money created from nothing.

cards.prompt: You need to fix one customer's email in production by hand. How do you avoid the classic `UPDATE` without `WHERE` disaster?
cards.answer: Run the `WHERE` as a `SELECT` first and check the row count; open a transaction, run the `UPDATE`, confirm the reported affected-row count matches, then `COMMIT` (or `ROLLBACK`). Use a role with only the permissions needed, and prefer a reviewed migration or admin tool over ad-hoc SQL.
cards.explanation: Safety nets exist too: MySQL's `--safe-updates` rejects UPDATE and DELETE without a key in the WHERE clause, and some clients warn before running them. Point-in-time recovery is the last resort — slow and disruptive, so rely on it least.

modules.name: Aggregation, Sets & Upserts
modules.description: GROUP BY and HAVING, set operators, EXISTS, CASE and COALESCE, upserts and keyset pagination.

cards.prompt: What rows does this return?
cards.code:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE orders (customer TEXT, amount INT);
INSERT INTO orders VALUES
  ('ada', 50), ('ada', 70), ('bob', 20), ('cy', 90), ('cy', 5);
""")
for row in db.execute("""
SELECT customer, COUNT(*), SUM(amount)
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer
HAVING SUM(amount) > 50
ORDER BY customer
"""):
    print(row)
cards.explanation: `GROUP BY` collapses rows into one per group; aggregates (`COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`) summarise each group. `WHERE` filters rows before grouping, `HAVING` filters groups after — so a condition on `SUM(amount)` must go in HAVING. Every selected column must be grouped or aggregated.

cards.prompt: `UNION` vs `UNION ALL`
cards.answer: `UNION` combines result sets and removes duplicates; `UNION ALL` keeps every row.

left.title: UNION
points: Needs a sort or hash — extra cost
Correct when overlap must be removed

right.title: UNION ALL
points: Right default when sets are disjoint

cards.explanation: Removing duplicates needs a sort or hash over the whole result, so `UNION ALL` is much cheaper — use it whenever duplicates are impossible or wanted. `INTERSECT` and `EXCEPT` complete the set operators. All require the same number of columns with compatible types.

cards.prompt: When should you use `EXISTS` rather than `IN` or a JOIN?
cards.answer: Use `EXISTS` for "rows that have at least one related row" — it stops at the first match and never duplicates outer rows. A JOIN would multiply rows when there are several matches (needing DISTINCT), and `NOT IN` returns no rows at all if the subquery yields a NULL.
cards.explanation: `NOT EXISTS` is the safe anti-join: "customers with no orders" should be `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)`. Modern planners often turn IN and EXISTS into the same semi-join plan, so choose for correctness and clarity.

cards.prompt: What rows does this return?
cards.code:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE orders (customer TEXT, amount INT);
INSERT INTO orders VALUES
  ('ada', 50), ('ada', 70), ('bob', 20), ('cy', 90), ('cy', 5);
CREATE TABLE customers (name TEXT);
INSERT INTO customers VALUES ('ada'), ('bob'), ('cy'), ('dee');
""")
for row in db.execute("""
SELECT c.name,
       CASE WHEN COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) >= 90 THEN 'big' ELSE 'small' END,
       COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0)
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer = c.name
GROUP BY c.name
ORDER BY c.name
"""):
    print(row)
cards.answer:
('ada', 'big', 120)
('bob', 'small', 20)
('cy', 'big', 95)
('dee', 'small', 0)
cards.explanation: `CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END` is SQL's conditional expression, usable anywhere a value is. `COALESCE(a, b, ...)` returns the first non-NULL argument — here it turns the missing total for a customer with no orders into 0. The LEFT JOIN keeps `dee` despite having no orders.

cards.prompt: You need "insert this row, or update it if the key already exists" — safely under concurrency. How?
cards.answer: A native upsert: `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET ...` in PostgreSQL and SQLite, `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` in MySQL, `MERGE` in SQL Server and others. It relies on a unique constraint and is atomic.
cards.explanation: The hand-rolled "SELECT, then INSERT or UPDATE" races: two requests both see no row and both insert, producing a duplicate or a constraint error. Let the unique constraint arbitrate — it is the only part of the system that sees every concurrent writer.

resources.title: PostgreSQL docs — INSERT — ON CONFLICT clause

cards.prompt: Page 5,000 of this feed takes seconds. What is the problem and the SQL fix?
cards.code:
SELECT id, title, created_at
FROM posts
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000;
cards.answer: `OFFSET 100000` still reads and discards 100,000 rows. Use keyset (seek) pagination: remember the last row's sort key and continue after it — `WHERE (created_at, id) < ($last_ts, $last_id) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20` — which an index on `(created_at, id)` serves directly.
cards.explanation: The `id` tiebreaker makes the order total, so rows with equal timestamps are neither skipped nor repeated. Keyset pages stay fast at any depth and are stable while new rows arrive; the trade-off is no jumping to an arbitrary page number.

resources.title: Use The Index, Luke — Paging through results

cards.prompt: What do FULL OUTER, CROSS and self joins do?
cards.answer: FULL OUTER keeps unmatched rows from both sides, padding with NULLs — useful for reconciling two sources. CROSS JOIN pairs every row with every row (a Cartesian product), for generating combinations. A self join joins a table to itself under two aliases — employees to their managers, or rows to their neighbours.
cards.explanation: An accidental Cartesian product — a missing or wrong join condition — is a classic way to turn a small query into millions of rows. If a result count looks like the product of two table sizes, check the ON clause first.

modules.name: Schema, Constraints & Advanced Indexing
modules.description: Keys and constraints, views, covering and partial indexes, triggers and procedures, and ORMs.

cards.prompt: Which constraints should a schema use, and why enforce them in the database rather than only in code?
cards.answer: PRIMARY KEY (unique row identity), FOREIGN KEY (references must exist), UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK (row-level rules such as `amount >= 0`) and, in Postgres, EXCLUDE (no overlapping ranges).
cards.explanation: Application checks race and get bypassed by scripts, migrations and other services; constraints hold for every writer, always. They also document the model and help the planner. Index foreign-key columns — deletes on the parent otherwise scan the child table.

cards.prompt: Surrogate keys vs natural keys
cards.answer: A natural key comes from the data itself (email, ISBN, country code); a surrogate key is a meaningless generated identifier (auto-increment integer, UUID).

right.title: Surrogate key
points: Keep a UNIQUE on the natural key too

cards.explanation: Natural keys change more often than anyone expects — people change emails, and "unique" business codes get reused — and every change cascades through foreign keys. The common pattern is a surrogate primary key plus a UNIQUE constraint on the natural key. For UUIDs prefer time-ordered UUIDv7, which keeps B-tree inserts local.

cards.prompt: View vs materialised view
cards.answer: A view is a stored query, re-run every time it is read; a materialised view stores the query's result and must be refreshed.

left.title: View
points: A named query, no stored data
Only as fast as the underlying query
Good for abstraction and access control

right.title: Materialised view
points: Good for dashboards and heavy aggregates

cards.explanation: Views give abstraction and security (expose a subset of columns) at no storage cost. Materialised views make expensive aggregations cheap to read at the price of staleness and refresh cost — `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY` avoids blocking readers in Postgres.

cards.prompt: What is a covering (index-only) scan, and how do you get one?
cards.answer: When every column a query needs is in the index, the database answers from the index alone without visiting the table rows. Add the extra columns to the index key, or as non-key payload with `INCLUDE (col)` in Postgres and SQL Server.
cards.explanation: It avoids a random heap lookup per matching row — often the dominant cost. In Postgres it also depends on the visibility map being current (vacuumed). `SELECT *` defeats it, which is one more reason to select only the columns you need.

resources.title: Use The Index, Luke — Index-only scan

cards.prompt: Only 1% of orders are `pending`, and every dashboard query filters `WHERE status = 'pending'`. Also, logins look up users by `lower(email)`. Which indexes?
cards.answer: A partial index — `CREATE INDEX ON orders (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending'` — indexes only the 1% you query, keeping it tiny. An expression index — `CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email))` — lets the planner use an index for the function call.
cards.explanation: A plain index on `email` cannot serve `WHERE lower(email) = ...`, because the indexed values differ from the expression. Partial unique indexes also enforce rules like "only one active subscription per user".

cards.prompt: Should business logic live in triggers and stored procedures?
cards.answer: Sparingly. Keep integrity rules that must hold for every writer in the database — constraints first, triggers for audit trails or derived columns. Keep business workflows in application code, where they are versioned, tested, reviewed and observable like everything else.
cards.explanation: Triggers act invisibly: a simple UPDATE can cascade into unexpected work, and they are hard to test and debug. Stored procedures earn their place for set-based operations close to the data or where many applications must share one guarded interface.

cards.prompt: ORM vs raw SQL / query builder
cards.answer: An ORM maps tables to objects and generates SQL; raw SQL or a thin query builder keeps you writing the queries yourself.
cards.explanation: Use the ORM for routine CRUD and drop to SQL for reports, bulk operations and anything performance-critical. Whatever you use, log the generated SQL in development and watch query counts per request — most ORM problems are invisible until you look at what it actually sent.
